problem: Wires need strain relief inside an enclosure without exterior leak paths.
solution: Use a low wall-side wire lane with bridge-style cable-tie saddles. The tie passes through an internal pass-under tunnel while the exterior wall remains solid.

problem: External enclosure mounts need strength and clean appearance.
solution: Use a rounded lug with screw boss, broad neck, and clean gussets into the wall/floor.

problem: Printed plastic needs durable threaded PCB or enclosure fasteners.
solution: Use a supported boss with insert pilot hole, base pad, insert depth, and gussets.

problem: Wires need to enter an enclosure that may need dust or water resistance.
solution: Use one circular hole sized for a grommet or cable gland with a reinforcing boss or ring.

problem: PCB screws need support under vibration without damaging the board.
solution: Use standoffs aligned to actual PCB holes with base pads, insert holes, and gussets.

problem: Wires need a controlled path from entry point to solder pads.
solution: Use low internal routing pads or channels that guide wires without blocking PCB installation.

problem: A PCB carrier needs protection without excessive size.
solution: Use compact margins, meaningful walls, reinforced floor, service access, and intentional mounting features.

problem: Enclosure features can be wrong if PCB dimensions and holes are guessed.
solution: Extract board outline, mounting holes, component heights, and connector zones from source PCB files before modeling.

problem: A strong external mount still looks crude if it uses forked tabs, random fins, or patched-on blocks.
solution: Use an oval or teardrop lug with a centered screw hole, raised boss, wide blended neck into the wall or floor, and two simple clean gussets.

problem: A functional OpenSCAD enclosure can still look blocky or hobby-grade because walls, rims, bosses, and internal features use inconsistent geometry.
solution: Refine style by using a continuous rounded wall shell, subtle top rim cap, stepped grommet boss, shared softened feature radii, and cleaner transitions while preserving fixed PCB and fastener geometry.

problem: Wire strain relief fails when a zip-tie feature has no real pass-through path or creates exterior leak holes.
solution: Use a floor-mounted internal bridge with two side feet, a top strap, and an explicit rectangular tunnel clearance. Show the tunnel with a preview block and keep the exterior wall solid.

problem: A zip-tie saddle can have a tunnel but still be impossible to use after the PCB and wires are installed.
solution: Place open-top saddles in the accessible channel between PCB edge and inside wall, with previewed clearance to both. Use visible tie path and wire bundle previews so the feature can be checked with the PCB installed.

problem: A slot or tunnel may look real but not pass through the feature body.
solution: Build the feature body and a separate tunnel_cut() module, then subtract the cut with difference(). Extend the cut slightly beyond the target body in the travel direction.
avoid: cuts that do not intersect the solid

problem: PCB-derived features are misplaced when enclosure offsets are typed manually in many modules.
solution: Define pcb_origin_x and pcb_origin_y once, then use pcb_x() and pcb_y() helper functions for mounting holes, wire zones, keepouts, and previews.

problem: A CAD model can render but still hide blocked paths or inaccessible service features.
solution: Use optional transparent preview geometry for PCBs, wire bundles, zip-tie paths, screw access, and clearance envelopes.

problem: Wire entry cutouts can become random wall gaps or weak openings.
solution: Create a circular through-wall cut using a rotated cylinder and reinforce it with a separate boss or ring around the hole.

problem: Insert bosses split or pull out when they are isolated skinny cylinders.
solution: Use a boss with adequate OD, insert pilot cut, base pad, and ribs or gussets tying it into the floor or wall.

problem: External mount tabs look crude or fail under vibration when modeled as flat ears.
solution: Use a hull-based rounded lug, centered screw cut, raised boss, wide neck, and simple load-path gussets.

problem: Files become hard to debug when feature bodies and cuts are mixed randomly.
solution: Use a main assembly where production solids are grouped in union() and all named cut modules are subtracted in the surrounding difference().

problem: Large SCAD files become fragile when parameters, helpers, features, previews, and final calls are interleaved.
solution: Use fixed sections: header, source facts, adjustable parameters, preview toggles, derived dimensions, helpers, body, features, cutouts, previews, main assembly, final call.

problem: Floor-mounted tie saddles can be hard to reach after PCB installation, while through-wall tie slots create leak paths.
solution: Add an inward pad to the inside wall and cut upper/lower slots only through that pad, leaving a solid center bridge for the zip tie and keeping the exterior wall uncut.
avoid: cutting slots through the exterior wall
floor tunnels hidden by the PCB

problem: A serviceable wall zip-tie feature can make an enclosure too wide if side clearance is guessed instead of calculated.
solution: Compute side margin from wall thickness, wall-tie pad projection, tie clearance, wire lane width, and PCB-edge clearance. Derive wire-lane positions from the PCB origin and show preview blocks for lane and tie path.
avoid: wire lanes that are not previewed
